title: Bidirectional BFS vs Milan streets: meet in the middle!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS carve through Milan’s street graph by expanding frontiers from both start and goal simultaneously. The visualization highlights how meeting in the middle can cut search work compared to one-direction BFS.
ig_caption:
🗺️🚦 Milan (Navigli) street map + **Bidirectional BFS** = faster routes!

In graph theory terms, we model intersections as nodes and streets as edges (often unweighted). **Bidirectional BFS** runs two BFS searches at the same time: one from the start node and one from the goal node. As layers expand outward, the searches “meet” when they touch the same node (or connect across edges), drastically reducing the explored area—especially on large, sparse graphs where shortest paths exist.

✨ On a real street-map layout, this means fewer expansions than standard BFS: instead of sweeping the whole wavefront from one side, we shrink the problem by meeting in the middle. The result is a clean visualization of shortest-path discovery driven by level-order traversal.

fb_caption:
🚗💡 Exploring shortest paths on a real street graph! Using **Bidirectional BFS**, we run two breadth-first searches—one from the start and one from the destination—until the frontiers meet. This is a classic graph search optimization: fewer explored nodes while still guaranteeing the shortest path on unweighted maps.
